source.title: Data Selection via Optimal Control for Language Models
source.authors: Yu-Xian Gu; Li Dong; Hong-Ning Wang; Y. Hao; Qing-Xiu Dong; Fu-Ru Wei; Minlie Huang

record.tranche_reason: The paper measures held-out language-model losses over model size and training tokens and fits a scaling-law form, using its own training setup rather than reproducing the original studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling-law fits and goodness-of-fit values, which bear on V1 and V7, and downstream accuracy scaling curves relevant to V6. The losses extrapolated to GPT-3 and Llama-scale configurations are predictions only, not evaluations of runs at those scales. Cited scaling-law results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: This is a data-selection paper (PDS). It fits a Hoffmann-style L(N,D) law to its own DCLM test losses only to project PDS gains to GPT-3/Llama scales (Table 3) and to estimate data savings. The scaling law is a tool. The fit spans about one order of magnitude in parameters (160M–1.7B) and 2.5B–50B tokens. Its in-sample R² checks (Table 9) are not tests of a power law over several orders of magnitude. No extrapolation is checked against real large runs, so V2 is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that PDS-selected data speeds up LM learning (about 2x on 1.7B) and improves downstream and DCLM loss performance across 160M–1.7B. They extrapolate with a fitted Hoffmann-style law that gains persist for ~400B models on ~15T tokens. They also find PDS cuts data demand 1.8x in data-constrained settings. The scaling law is used as a projection tool, not tested.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the reported Hoffmann-style joint scaling-law form on this paper's own loss trajectories; the authors use a two-stage fitting procedure after finding the LBFGS fit sensitive to initialization. This is not an explicit replication of the original scaling-law experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that LBFGS fitting is sensitive to parameter initialization and use a two-stage fit: first fit data curves by nonlinear least squares, then initialize the joint fit. Fitted exponents also differ between conventional and PDS-selected data.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted exponents differ between conventional and PDS-selected data (α 0.397 vs 0.518; β 0.651 vs 0.585). Both fits share E=2.829 and carry no uncertainty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining data selection changes the fitted scaling-law exponents.

record.problems: The model-size range is 160M to 1.7B parameters. Large-scale losses in Table 3 are extrapolations, not measured outcomes. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the fitted constants or projected losses. The paper notes sensitivity of LBFGS to initialization and changes its fitting procedure.

untested.parts: Power law across several orders of magnitude; compute scaling; held-out validation of the fit.
All parts. Table 3 losses are extrapolations never compared with real runs.
All parts. The multi-epoch data-constrained extrapolation uses the Muennighoff law as a tool.
Comparison of fitting methods, comparison across published laws, and curve bending. The data-dependence of exponents is not established without uncertainty.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's labels (V1 supports/limits_scope, V6 limits_scope, V7 supports) are withdrawn because the study uses the law without testing it. The R² values are computed on transformed, in-sample data with fitted E and A/N^α plugged in, so they overstate fit quality. The text calls the constants Table 9 but prints them in Figure 9. The LBFGS initialization sensitivity is an anecdotal fitting remark with no comparison of results across methods.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary compute independently of model size and token count, and tests model sizes only from 160M to 1.7B parameters.
The large-run loss values are extrapolations; the paper does not compare those predictions with actual larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split is measured.
Architecture details are not varied at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text pre-training and does not test other modalities, repeated-data regimes as a general scaling law, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The study plots downstream accuracy against model size and compute, but does not establish a predictive mapping from pre-training loss to downstream performance.

The paper does not test compute-optimal allocation, systematic curve bending, or disagreement among published laws. It reports different fitted exponents for conventional and PDS data, but does not compare exponent estimates across fitting methods.

rows.subject: Conventional
rows.operation_detail: Fit the reported joint loss scaling law to DCLM test losses over model sizes and training-token counts.
rows.note: The constants are printed in the figure; the fit uses losses from 160M, 470M, 1B, and 1.7B models during training.
rows.check: These are fitted constants, not an effect. They differ from r2, but no uncertainty is given. E is identical (2.829) in both fits, and the authors say LBFGS is sensitive to initialization. The exponent gap cannot be read as a data effect on exponents. Not evidence for V1 on its own.
